4º de Primaria · Inglés · Tema 10

Reading and writing a short story

Nombre: ______________________   Fecha: ___________

Qué vas a aprender

  • Recognise the parts of a story: beginning, middle and end
  • Identify characters, setting and problem
  • Use linking words: once upon a time, one day, suddenly, finally
  • Plan and write a short story of your own
  • Describe characters with adjectives of personality
  • Use common irregular verbs in the past
  • Read fables and find their moral
  • Write dialogues with speech marks and use story starters and endings

Para pensar

Casi todos los cuentos que conoces empiezan igual: «Érase una vez…». ¿Sabes cómo empiezan los cuentos en inglés?

Explicación

1. What is a story?

A story tells us about things that happen to some characters in a place. Stories can be real or invented, funny or scary, about animals, kids, monsters or robots. Fairy tales, fables and comics are all kinds of stories.

Every good story has three ingredients: who (the characters), where and when (the setting) and what happens (the plot). En castellano: story es «cuento» o «historia»; tale también es cuento, y fairy tale es un cuento de hadas.

2. Characters and setting

The characters are the people or animals in the story. The main character (protagonista) is the most important one. We describe characters with adjectives: brave (valiente), shy (tímido), clever (listo), kind (amable), naughty (travieso), grumpy (gruñón).

The setting is where and when the story happens: in a dark forest, in a castle, at school, on a spaceship, a long time ago, last summer… Consejo: un buen escenario ayuda al lector a imaginar la historia.

3. Describing characters

Good stories have interesting characters. To describe them, we can talk about their appearance (what they look like) and their personality (what they are like).

Appearance:

  • tall, short, big, small, thin, strong
  • long / short / curly / straight hair
  • «The giant was enormous and he had a long grey beard.»

Personality (positive):

  • brave (valiente), kind (amable), clever (listo), friendly (simpático), generous, honest (sincero), funny (gracioso), hard-working (trabajador).

Personality (negative):

  • greedy (avaricioso), lazy (perezoso), selfish (egoísta), mean (malo, tacaño), rude (maleducado), proud (orgulloso), bossy (mandón).

In many stories, there's a hero (the main character) and a villain (the bad character). The hero is usually brave and kind; the villain is greedy or mean.

Tip: don't just say «He was nice». Show it with an action: «He gave his last piece of bread to a hungry dog.» Now the reader knows he is generous!

In the reading, the mouse is brave and loyal, and the lion is proud at first, but then he's grateful (agradecido).

4. Beginning, middle and end

Stories have three parts. In the beginning we meet the characters and the setting: «Once upon a time, there was a little robot called Bip». In the middle there is a problem: «One day, Bip lost his battery». In the end the problem is solved: «Finally, his friend found it and Bip was happy again».

En castellano: es el mismo esquema que en Lengua: planteamiento, nudo y desenlace. Sin problema no hay historia: ¡algo tiene que salir mal para que la aventura sea interesante!

5. Linking words

Linking words help us tell the events in order. To start: Once upon a time (érase una vez), One day (un día), Long ago (hace mucho tiempo). To continue: Then (luego), Next, After that. For a surprise: Suddenly (de repente).

To finish: In the end, Finally (al final) and The end (fin). Consejo: Suddenly es la palabra mágica para presentar el problema: «Suddenly, a big storm started…». ¡Engancha al lector!

6. Stories in the past

Most stories are told in the past. You don't need to know all the past tenses yet, but these verbs appear in almost every story: was / were (era, estaba), there was (había), lived (vivía), wanted (quería), went (fue), saw (vio), said (dijo), found (encontró), had (tenía).

Example: «Once upon a time, there was a girl who lived near the sea. One day she went to the beach and saw a bottle». Read them as words and you'll understand the story perfectly.

7. Irregular verbs in stories

Many verbs in English add -ed in the past: walk → walked, play → played, shout → shouted. But the most common verbs in stories are irregular: they change completely! Learn these by heart:

  • go → went (fue)
  • see → saw (vio)
  • say → said (dijo)
  • have → had (tenía, tuvo)
  • come → came (vino)
  • find → found (encontró)
  • run → ran (corrió)
  • take → took (cogió)
  • eat → ate (comió)
  • make → made (hizo)
  • give → gave (dio)
  • get → got (consiguió, llegó)
  • fall → fell (cayó)
  • catch → caught (atrapó)
  • hear → heard (oyó)
  • be → was / were (era, estaba)

Good news: in the past, the verb is the same for everybody: «I went, you went, she went, they went». No -s for he and she!

Look at this paragraph: «One day, Jack went to the market. He saw an old man. The man gave him some magic beans. Jack took them home.» Find the irregular verbs in the reading!

8. Reading: The Little Cloud

Read this story: «Once upon a time, there was a little cloud called Nimbo. He lived high in the sky with his family. Nimbo was very shy. The other clouds made big storms, but he only made a tiny drop of rain. One day, he saw a small village with a dry garden. The flowers were sad and brown. Suddenly, Nimbo had an idea. He said: "I can help!". He cried and cried, very softly. Finally, the flowers opened and the children danced in the rain. Nimbo wasn't shy any more. The end.»

9. Understanding the story

Let's analyse «The Little Cloud». Characters: Nimbo (the main character), his family, the flowers and the children. Setting: the sky and a small village. Beginning: Nimbo is a shy little cloud. Problem: the garden is dry and the flowers are sad. End: Nimbo makes gentle rain and the flowers open.

What's the message of the story? Maybe: «Small things can help a lot» or «Everyone is good at something». Pregunta: ¿qué palabra presenta la idea de Nimbo? (Suddenly).

10. Fables and their morals

A fable (fábula) is a short story, usually with animals that talk and act like people. At the end, there's a moral (moraleja): a lesson about how to behave.

The most famous writer of fables is Aesop, who lived in ancient Greece about 2,500 years ago. Here are some of his fables:

  • The Tortoise and the Hare (La tortuga y la liebre): the hare is very fast but very proud. He stops to sleep during a race, and the slow tortoise wins. Moral: Slow and steady wins the race.
  • The Ant and the Grasshopper (La hormiga y la cigarra): the ant works all summer and saves food. The grasshopper only sings and plays. In winter, the grasshopper has no food. Moral: Work today and you will have tomorrow.
  • The Boy Who Cried Wolf (Pedro y el lobo): a shepherd boy lies about a wolf many times. When a real wolf comes, nobody believes him. Moral: Nobody believes a liar, even when he tells the truth.
  • The Fox and the Grapes (La zorra y las uvas): a fox can't reach some grapes, so he says they're sour. Moral: It's easy to hate what you can't have.

Fables are told all over the world. In Spain, the writer Félix María de Samaniego wrote fables in verse, and in France, Jean de La Fontaine wrote very famous ones.

To find the moral, ask: What did the character learn? What can I learn from the story?

11. Planning your own story

Before writing, make a story map (esquema). Answer these questions: Who is the main character? What is he/she like? Where does the story happen? What is the problem? How is it solved?

Ideas: a dragon who is afraid of fire, a cat who wants to be an astronaut, a pencil that draws by itself, a girl who finds a secret door in the library. Consejo: elige una sola idea y un solo problema. Los mejores cuentos cortos son sencillos.

12. Writing your story

Now write your story in three paragraphs, about 60 to 80 words. Paragraph 1: «Once upon a time, there was… He/She lived in…». Paragraph 2: «One day… Suddenly…». Paragraph 3: «Finally… The end».

Check your work with this list: Does it have a title? Are there capital letters at the start of sentences and for names? Did you use full stops (.)? Did you use at least three linking words? Then illustrate it and read it aloud to a younger class. ¡Ya eres escritor en inglés!

13. Dialogue in stories

Dialogue (the words the characters say) makes stories more alive. In English, we write dialogue with speech marks (comillas): "…".

Look at these rules:

  • Put the exact words inside the speech marks: "Help me!" said the mouse.
  • Start a new line every time a different character speaks.
  • Put the punctuation (, ? !) inside the speech marks: "Where are you going?" asked the wolf.
  • Use a comma before the closing speech mark if the sentence continues: "I'm hungry," said the bear.

Instead of said every time, use more interesting speaking verbs:

  • asked (preguntó): for questions.
  • answered / replied (respondió).
  • shouted / cried (gritó).
  • whispered (susurró).
  • laughed (rió).
  • roared (rugió): for a lion!

Example:

"Who's there?" whispered Lucy.
"It's me, Tom," replied a voice.
"Tom! You scared me!" laughed Lucy.

Notice that in Spanish we use a dash (—) for dialogue, but in English we use speech marks.

14. Story starters and endings

The first and the last sentences of a story are very important. A good beginning makes the reader want to continue, and a good ending leaves the reader happy or surprised.

Story starters:

  • Once upon a time… (Érase una vez): perfect for fairy tales.
  • A long time ago, in a faraway land…
  • One cold winter morning…
  • It was a dark and stormy night…
  • Nobody believed me when I said…

Words for the middle: One day, Suddenly, Then, After that, Later, At that moment, Meanwhile (mientras tanto).

Story endings:

  • …and they lived happily ever after. (…y vivieron felices para siempre.)
  • In the end, they became best friends.
  • Finally, everybody went home, tired but happy.
  • From that day on, she never lied again.
  • And that's why the elephant has a long trunk!

Remember the plan: beginning (characters and setting) → middle (a problem) → end (the solution).

Challenge: choose a starter, a problem and an ending, and write a story of three paragraphs!

The parts of a story

Ejercicios

  1. How do stories start in English?

  2. Translate: personaje, escenario, problema.

  3. What are the three parts of a story?

  4. Which linking word introduces a surprise?

  5. Translate: valiente, tímido, travieso.

  6. Who is the main character in «The Little Cloud»?

  7. What is the problem in «The Little Cloud»?

  8. Translate: «Había un perro que vivía en un castillo.»

  9. Write a beginning for a story about a robot.

  10. Write an ending with «Finally».

  11. Write the past of go and see.

  12. What is a fable?

  13. Opposite of brave?

  14. How do fairy tales often start?

  15. Write a speaking verb for questions.

  16. What is the moral of The Tortoise and the Hare?

  17. Write the past: The mouse runs and finds the lion.

  18. Describe the lion in the reading with two adjectives.

  19. Punctuate: Where are you going asked the wolf

  20. Write two story endings.

  21. Write a fable with two animals and a moral.

  22. Rewrite the lion and the mouse from the mouse's point of view.

  23. Write a dialogue between a hero and a villain.

  24. Write a story with five irregular verbs in the past.

Practica

  1. «Érase una vez» is…

    1. A) One time ago
    2. B) There was one day
    3. C) Once upon a time

  2. The characters are…

    1. A) the people or animals in the story
    2. B) the place
    3. C) the title

  3. The setting is…

    1. A) the problem
    2. B) where and when the story happens
    3. C) the end

  4. Which part has the problem?

    1. A) the beginning
    2. B) the middle
    3. C) the title

  5. «Suddenly» means…

    1. A) al final
    2. B) érase
    3. C) de repente

  6. «Brave» means…

    1. A) valiente
    2. B) tímido
    3. C) gruñón

  7. Which is a word to finish?

    1. A) One day
    2. B) Once upon a time
    3. C) Finally

  8. «There was» means…

    1. A) hay
    2. B) había
    3. C) habrá

  9. In «The Little Cloud», Nimbo is…

    1. A) shy
    2. B) grumpy
    3. C) naughty

  10. At the start of a sentence we use…

    1. A) a capital letter
    2. B) a full stop
    3. C) a question mark

  11. The past of «take» is…

    1. A) taked
    2. B) took
    3. C) taken

  12. A person who never wants to work is…

    1. A) brave
    2. B) kind
    3. C) lazy

  13. The lesson of a fable is the…

    1. A) setting
    2. B) moral
    3. C) title

  14. In English, dialogue goes in…

    1. A) speech marks
    2. B) dashes
    3. C) brackets

  15. «…and they lived happily ever after» is…

    1. A) a starter
    2. B) a title
    3. C) an ending

Explícalo con tus palabras

Incluye: Qué ingredientes tiene un cuento; Qué son los personajes y el escenario; Las tres partes de un cuento y para qué sirve el problema; Los conectores para empezar, seguir y terminar.

Tarjetas de repaso

Recórtalas: pregunta delante, respuesta detrás.

Once upon a timeÉrase una vez.
characterPersonaje.
settingLugar y tiempo del cuento.
beginning / middle / endPrincipio / nudo / desenlace.
problemLo que sale mal en el nudo.
SuddenlyDe repente.
FinallyAl final.
The endFin.
CharactersHero: brave, kind. Villain: greedy, mean.

FablesAnimals + a moral. Aesop.
Dialogue and endings"Help!" cried the mouse. …happily ever after.

Soluciones

  1. C) Fórmula de inicio.
  2. A) Personajes.
  3. B) Escenario.
  4. B) Nudo.
  5. C) Sorpresa.
  6. A) brave.
  7. C) Final.
  8. B) Pasado.
  9. A) Tímido.
  10. A) Mayúscula.
  11. B) Irregular verbs.
  12. C) Characters.
  13. B) Fables.
  14. A) Dialogue.
  15. C) Starters and endings.
